title: A 55-year-old female presents with a chief complaint of severe excruciating pain and points to the region of her right face, infraorbital foramen, right nose, right upper lip and the apex of #6.  She describes her pain as extremely severe indicating it is like a “jolt of lightening,“ lasting approximately 5 seconds, then slowly subsides.  These painful episodes are occurring repeatedly throughout the day (she estimates approximately 50-100 per day).  She indicates that the pain is brought on by brushing her teeth, putting on lipstick and wind on her face.  The examination findings demonstrate that tooth #6 is extremely painful to touch, and when you perform percussion on #6, she screams in severe pain. Radiographs demonstrate a crown on #6 with previous endodontic therapy and a very small apical lucency.  The intraoral examination is essentially unremarkable in the region of #6 (no swelling, no fistula, no purulence, no periodontal disease). title: A 43-year-old male presents to your office with pain, pointing to the region of the left mandible for 9 months.  He was initially diagnosed with a pulpitis associated with tooth #19 and following endodontic therapy, the symptoms improved slightly for one week then returned.  One month later he underwent an apicoectomy on #19 but the symptoms persisted.  Two months later he underwent extraction of #19 as well as #18, which had moderate periodontal disease.  The symptoms persisted and he was referred to a dentist who sees patients with temporomandibular disorders.  He was treated with an oral appliance to be used at night, which he has been compliant with for the past 5 months, but the symptoms have persisted.  He comes to your office, now pointing to tooth #20 as the location of the pain and begs you to remove this tooth.  Periapical and panoramic radiographs reveal a crown on #20, but no evidence of periodontal or apical infection.  What would be the most appropriate treatment/management for this patient?
TMD & Orofacial Pain Midterm Exam (Sprin: Endodontic therapy on #20 and if symptoms persist, extraction of #20
tmd: Since the most likely diagnosis is osteomyelitis left mandible, refer the patient to an oral & maxillofacial surgeon for antibiotic therapy and possible extraction of #20 with bone biopsy
midterm: Referral to a center for the management of chronic orofacial pain with multiple specialists to assist in establishing the diagnosis, followed by appropriate management/treatment.
column5: All of the answer choices are appropriate in the treatment/management of this patient

title: A 22-year-old female has severe pain localized to the right TMJ with limited mandibular movement and deviation to the right upon jaw opening. She has no medical problems but indicates that she is under severe stress.
